pages.text: The young chief of Dadease Nkwanta, an invented town, sat alone with a lantern. On the table lay a letter and a roll of money. The letter offered a large payment for permission to bring machines onto the stool land and along the river. “Chiefs are custodians of the land,” his father had said. Tonight the word felt very heavy.

On the table lay a letter and a roll of money.
The letter offered a large payment for permission to bring machines onto the stool land and along the river.
“Chiefs are custodians of the land,” his father had said.
Tonight the word felt very heavy.
pages.alt: A young chief sits at a table by lantern light with a letter and a roll of money before him.

pages.text: The elders came first. One said, “The money could build a school block and a clinic. Other towns are doing it.” Another shook his head. “Money that comes this fast leaves just as fast, and takes the river with it.” The chief listened to both. “The National House of Chiefs says chiefs have opposed galamsey,” he said, “but also says that the present approach is not working and chiefs must be involved.”

Other towns are doing it.” Another shook his head.
“Money that comes this fast leaves just as fast, and takes the river with it.” The chief listened to both.
“The National House of Chiefs says chiefs have opposed galamsey,” he said, “but also says that the present approach is not working and chiefs must be involved.”
pages.alt: Elders sit in a circle under a lantern, some leaning forward, some with arms folded.

pages.text: Then the queen mother, Nana Ohemaa, spoke. “Who owns the river, Nana?” she asked. “The town,” said the chief. “Is the town only the people alive today?” she said. “Our ancestors gave us this land. Our grandchildren will need it. A custodian does not own. A custodian keeps. If we sell the river, we sell what was lent to us.” The chief lowered his eyes.

Our grandchildren will need it.
A custodian does not own.
A custodian keeps.
If we sell the river, we sell what was lent to us.” The chief lowered his eyes.
pages.alt: A queen mother in gold beads speaks calmly to the chief while the lantern flickers between them.

pages.text: A farmer was next. “My cassava is yellow,” he said. “The stream I use is brown. Doctors say crops and fish in galamsey areas can carry chemicals. We eat what we grow, Nana.” Then a young man named Kwaw spoke quietly. “I have no job. The diggers pay. If you say no, what do you offer me instead?” The room was silent. It was the best question of the night.

pages.text: Last, Naa Dorcas stepped forward with her notebook. “Nana,” she said, “our class has been reading about this. In December 2025 the law was changed so that mining in forest reserves is banned and breaking it can bring fifteen to twenty-five years in prison. The law also says that people who help or hide illegal miners can be punished too. If you say yes, you could be breaking the law as well as harming the river.”

“Nana,” she said, “our class has been reading about this.
In December 2025 the law was changed so that mining in forest reserves is banned and breaking it can bring fifteen to twenty-five years in prison.
The law also says that people who help or hide illegal miners can be punished too.
If you say yes, you could be breaking the law as well as harming the river.”
pages.alt: A schoolgirl with a notebook speaks to the chief as elders listen.

pages.text: “Some reports say that a few chiefs have taken money from machine owners,” Naa Dorcas went on, “and that is a serious claim. But reports also say that many chiefs and traditional councils want to be part of the solution. Which kind of chief will you be, Nana?” The chief smiled sadly. “You are a brave child,” he said. “And you have given me a problem I cannot send away.”

“You are a brave child,” he said.
“And you have given me a problem I cannot send away.”
pages.alt: A chief looks at a schoolgirl and then at the river through the window, thoughtful.

pages.text: Before dawn, the chief made up his mind. He called a durbar. He said no to the letter and the money. “But my no is not enough,” he said. “We will make a bylaw to protect the river and the farms. We will plant trees along the banks. We will ask the Assembly and the Minerals Commission for help to open a legal route for those who want to mine safely and with licences. And we will find work for our young people in farming, crafts and tree planting.”

We will ask the Assembly and the Minerals Commission for help to open a legal route for those who want to mine safely and with licences.
And we will find work for our young people in farming, crafts and tree planting.”
pages.alt: A durbar under a big tree with the chief addressing the crowd and a banner reading Protect Our River.

pages.text: Kwaw was the first to join the tree-planting team. “It pays less,” he said, “but it will still be here when my children are grown.” Naa Dorcas drew a picture of the river with trees on its banks and pinned it to the school wall. The chief looked at it for a long time. “Custodian,” he said softly. “Now I understand the word.” The end.

activities.question: What does the queen mother say a custodian does?
options: Keeps the land for those who come after

activities.prompt: Kwaw asks what he can do instead of mining. How might the chief answer?
options: By offering other work and a lawful route

activities.question: What does the chief do in the end?
options: Refuses the money and makes a bylaw to protect the river

activities.definition: A person who looks after something that belongs to everyone, or to the future.

items: Elders, the queen mother, a farmer and a young man speak.
The chief calls a durbar and announces a bylaw.

activities.prompt: Leaders sometimes have to choose what is right over what is easy. How does that feel?

glossary.definition: A person who looks after something for others and for the future.
A public gathering where chiefs and the people meet.
A local rule made by a community or council.
Family members who lived long ago.
